chapter_theme: First songs at Swamimalai (சுவாமி மலை, also called Tiruverakam and Gurumalai; 1 of 3): pleas against craving and courtesans, against a life spent at patrons' gates and against Death's hour, and several prayers in Siddhanta vocabulary for jnana, union without difference and a silence beyond breath-yoga; the praise keeps to Murugan as guru, as Valli's lover, and as giver of Tamil verse.
structure_note: Courtesan and desire songs (202, 204, 213, 215); doctrinal pleas (203, 205, 211, 216); life's passing and Death (208, 212); initiation and the devotees' cry (207, 214); poetry and patronage (209, 210). Song 206 has no text in the source.

201.reading: The poet confesses that, not seeing that a life spent in the fire of craving for women is ruin, he grew deluded and never once thought of the name 'Sivaya', and asks Murugan to call him in his darkness and give him the feet that great ascetics meditate on, where the veiling impurity ends. The praise names the twelve-armed, six-faced son of Siva who rides the peacock with the vel in hand, the lover of the hunters' doe, and the lord of Swamimalai to whom Indra, Brahma and Vishnu bow.
201.nuance: The first word, அவா (craving), sets the theme, and every line opens on a long syllable of the same pattern (அவா, அரா, சிவா, உவா, உலா, துவா, சுரா). திரோத மலம் is the veiling (tirodhana) counted among the impurities in Saiva doctrine. The opening words are hard to divide.

202.reading: The poet describes embracing women and drinking their lips' nectar, and asks that his craving for the pleasure of sinking like a worm into their navel cease, and that one day Murugan set his lotus feet as a crown on this dog-like servant's head and rule him with a word of teaching. The praise names the conqueror of the demon armies who commands the gods' host, twelve-armed Kanda whom the hunter girl of the rain-wet hill loves, the life of Vayalur, and the lord of Swamimalai of towers and golden walls.
202.nuance: கீடம்: the lover as a worm dying in a pit. The feet set on the head and a word of instruction (போதக வாசகம்) are the marks of a guru's initiation. Vayalur is named inside a Swamimalai song, as in 203.

203.reading: A doctrinal plea: the poet asks when, the fetter of earth and the darkness of great maya gone, he will reach the supreme light of consciousness, vast as space, which lies beyond the thirty-six tattvas and beyond turiya and which no master of yoga attains, and join with joy the unchanging, supportless Sthanu of bliss. The praise names Rama who bridged the sea and killed the ten-headed sinner as uncle, the son of Vayalur's Agnisvara, and the lover of the hunter girl, and asks for grace that ends the sense of 'mine'; the shrine is Swamimalai on the Kaveri's north bank.
203.nuance: ஆறாறின் அதிகம், beyond the thirty-six; பர துரியாதீதம், beyond turiya; பரை, the supreme Shakti; தாணு, Siva as the immovable. The whole plea is in Siddhanta's technical words, close to Tirumular's. The lines on the hunter girl and the eye-arrows that pierce the heart may speak of Murugan's love for Valli or of the poet's own heart; they are hard to divide.

204.reading: The poet lists women whose dark hair, eyes like Rama's arrows, musical speech, heavy breasts and vanishing waists wear down young men's hearts morning and evening while they name a price no one can meet, and asks that he not suffer in their love but be given the beginningless word of jnana that seeks the Lord's feet. The praise names Murugan whom devotees hail daily as Kumara in the shade of the kura tree, the vel that split Sura's hooded heads, and Swamimalai, where ascetics gather before whose good jnana deeds flee like straw before fire.
204.nuance: அடாத விலை கூறும்: naming an impossible price is what marks these women as courtesans. துரால் மிக தீ முன்: deeds burned like straw before fire, a common figure for knowledge destroying karma. அநாதி மொழி, 'the beginningless word', may mean the Veda or Om; the text does not say.

205.reading: The poet asks Murugan to come so that, the two deeds broken, the eye of jnana opened at its tip and the dark of impurity cleared, he and the six faces may mingle and the two become one without difference, while the gods bow, the women of heaven strew flowers and countless sages sing. The praise names Nataraja, whose red feet Vishnu and Brahma could not find, Siva of the three cities, whose body is like red-hot iron with the emerald woman at his side, and the vel that gave the enemies' lives to Death, at Swamimalai on the Kaveri's north bank.
205.nuance: பேதம் இலை என இரண்டு பேரும்: the goal is union without difference with the Lord, not only escape. அழலுறும் இரும்பின் மேனி ... மரகதம் பெண் ஆகம் அயல்: red Siva with green Uma at his side, the half-woman form. The first lines are partly garbled.

207.reading: The poet says he roamed, no one knowing anyone, tormented in the troubles of his two deeds, melting like wax in a furnace, dancing like a puppet on strings and vanishing like lightning, and asks Murugan, who came in form, spoke in his ears 'this is the supreme thing' and burned his karma and impurity to ash, to come on the peacock with his six compassionate faces and ringing anklets and rule him. The praise names Siva who burned the three cities and Kama, the dancer on the young bull, Arunagiri in form, the cause in Sivayanama, and calls Murugan the son of Uma, the poet's mother, the Kumaraguru the thousand Vedas hail, who joined Valli and Devayanai on Gurumalai.
207.nuance: என் செவியிணையின் அருளி உருவாகி வந்த: the song speaks of an initiation already given, the Lord coming in form and teaching in the poet's ears. Three images of a life driven by deeds: wax, a string-puppet, lightning. Siva is called அருணகிரி சொருபன், the form of Arunachala, which is also the poet's name.

208.reading: The poet sets out how uncertain life is: Yama on his buffalo, the messenger he sends whose path never fails, a story played in a dream, the wealth hunters hoard without giving; seeing that life does not stay, he asks Murugan to see that he too may chant him with sweet words morning and evening, today. The praise names Siva, lord of grammar, who dances daily with Pidari, the vel that ended Sura, and Swamimalai where ascetics in good jnana gather.
208.nuance: கிராதர் பொருள், wealth hunters gather and never give, stands beside the dream as a figure for what will not stay with you. வியாகரண ஈசன்: Siva as lord of grammar. The closing lines on breath and the five senses may describe the ascetics' restraint; the song shares its last line with 204.

209.reading: Mostly praise: Murugan wears the kadamba garland on twelve arms like Meru, bows his crown daily at the hunter girl's feet, delighted in Keeran's poems of true speech and taught him grammar, and by grace gives verse whose alliteration fits; the poet asks that grace grow daily on the mean words he speaks, and asks whether he must suffer here, lodged in this body like a nest in a bush. The shrine is Tiruverakam.
209.nuance: கீரன் is Nakkirar; the song makes Murugan his teacher of grammar (இலக்கணங்கள் இயல்பு ஓதி). அடிமோனை: the poet credits even his alliteration to grace. Murugan bowing his crown at Valli's feet reverses the usual order of worship.

210.reading: The poet asks whether he must wander, deluded, to the edges of the directions where the sun rises, the shores of the sea and the crown of the serpent king, wearing out his feet, never tiring of saying 'this is the place to sit near', and, when the powerful men he praised with music slip away, go to their gates night and day and wilt. The praise pictures bees in the areca blossoms and Sama singers at Swamimalai where the moon casts its shade, Murugan riding the peacock like a storm wind, and the son of the Mother who set all worlds in place.
210.nuance: இசையொடு புகழ்ந்த போது நழுவிய ப்ரசண்டர் வாசல்: the gates of patrons who slip away once they are praised in song, the same complaint as 220. The first lines may also describe wandering for wealth in general.

211.reading: The poet asks that the mind given to the anxious fancies of yoga go away, the yoga that refuses to think this stained body will not last, turns back the breath with ritual words and fans the inner fire; that the quarrelling five senses be uprooted and his own action end, so that he enters the full silence beyond qualities and reaches release; and he asks whether he will know, as the true guru of Gurumalai, the lotus feet on which he strews fresh flowers crying 'Kumara, refuge'. The praise tells of the war in which Murugan freed the gods to their city, burned the peaks and dried the sea, punished Brahma and kept him under guard, and married the elephant-raised Devayanai.
211.nuance: The participles (கருதுதல் ஒழிந்து, வாயுவை மறித்து, அனல் ஊதி, கவலைபடுகின்ற) appear to describe the yoga the poet wants to be rid of: a yoga of breath and fire aimed at keeping the body, set against the silence (மோனம்) beyond the gunas. Brahma's punishment (பிரமனை முனிந்து காவலிட்டு) is told without naming Om. Two corrupt glyphs.

212.reading: A short song: the poet asks not to waste away in desires nor die in the hands of Death's men, but, with love for the letter Om welling up, to be given the end 'in the painting'. The praise names the vel that drove off Sura, the hero on a peacock high as the golden mountain, and the lord at Erakam.
212.nuance: ஓவியத்தில் அந்தம் is obscure: it may be the stillness of a painted figure, an image for absorption. காமியம் may mean desire or rites done for desired ends. தூமமேய்க் கணிந்த in the praise is hard to read.

213.reading: The poet laments that he did not melt daily chanting Murugan's names, but wandered after cuckoo-voiced women who melt men with their eyes, walk the street as if lost in thought, seize their lovers' belongings, stand mid-street with garments slipping, net the penniless with their eyes and, having taken all, made him their slave doing whatever they bid; he asks for grace to praise the feet. The praise is a long battle with Virabhadras, Kali drinking blood, ghosts, jackals and vultures, and names Murugan of the Saiva faith, of Palani and Kathirkamam, dwelling at Tiruverakam.
213.nuance: அவர் அடிமை என மாதர் இட்ட தொழில் தனில் உழலும் அசடன்: the poet calls himself the women's slave, the bondage the other songs turn into service of the Lord. சிவசமய அறுமுக places Murugan within the Saiva faith. The battle is in drum syllables (திமிதமிட).

214.reading: The poet asks whether Murugan does not hear the cry for refuge of his devotees, crushed by cruel deeds, who chant him daily, 'Kumara, Guruparan, Muruga, Saravana, Guha, Shanmukha, younger brother of the elephant one, son of Siva, jewel of a guru', as gods once cried out at the sea. The praise names the peacock hero who felled the Suras, the guru of Siva whose feet took the life of Death and whose hair holds the river, and the lord of Gurumalai praised by the Vedas.
214.nuance: The plea is a litany of names, as if the song were itself the devotees' cry. நமனை உயிர்கொளும் இணைகழல்: Siva's feet that killed Yama, though the text names only the deed. The simile of the gods at the sea (அமுத இமையவர் திமிர்தம் இடு கடல்) is obscure.

215.reading: The poet asks whether he should keep company with courtesans who melt men's hearts, sell their lips daily, learn the calls of peacock, quail, cuckoo, dove and cock to bewitch with sidelong eyes, lie on flower beds, call anyone into their house, loosen their garments, embrace and snatch coins, and act out a learned art of deceit. The praise names the vel that cut down Sura, and lists the shrines where Murugan grants devotees all they wish, Kathirkamam, Palani, Tiruttani, Tiruchendur by the sea and Swamimalai called Erakam.
215.nuance: தோதக வித்தை படித்து நடிப்பவர்: deceit as a learned art and a performance. காசு பறிக்க மறித்து முயக்கிகள்: the embrace is for the coin. The praise is a pilgrim's list of shrines.

216.reading: The poet calls himself a dull, foolish wretch, born of worldly deeds, who never knew how to fix meditation on the lotus feet even for half a moment, and asks whether he must stay confused by poverty and what fault keeps Murugan from compassion now; he asks for great wealth, yoga, a life of greatness, Siva-jnana, release and the supreme state together. The praise names the son of Kailasa's lord who gave rare Tamil so the poet could praise his feet daily, and Murugan of Palani and Tiruverakam.
216.nuance: The plea sets worldly gifts beside final ones without embarrassment: wealth and yoga beside Siva-jnana and mukti. அரியதமிழ் தான் அளித்த: the gift of Tamil verse to praise the feet, as in 209. மிடி is poverty.

links.note: Tirumular teaches breath held on the left so that the body does not decay; 211 asks to be rid of the anxious yoga that turns back the breath because it will not accept that the body must go, and seeks silence instead. The conflict holds if 211's participles describe the yoga it rejects, which is the likelier reading.
Both use the string-puppet for a life with no inner agency: in the Kural the man without shame only seems alive, in 207 the poet dances on the strings of his two deeds.
Tirumular says the knowers perceive Siva within the soul 'like a painting'; 212's obscure plea for the end 'in the painting' may ask for the same still perception.
Both complain of the poet's life at patrons' gates: 210 of the men who slip away once praised in song, 220 of genres wasted on fools who toss a coin; both turn to the Lord's feet instead.

source_issues: Song 206 has no text (marked missing); the chapter runs 201-216 with 15 songs.
Song 203: the source's printed number is 202, duplicating song 202; one corrupt character in ப்஡ணதி (line 23), possibly ப்ரணதி or ப்ரீதி.
Song 211: two corrupt characters, அனலு஡தி (line 3, அனலூதி) and புண்ட஡ணகம் (line 12, புண்டரீகம், consistent with ஡ண for ரீ).
The source drops ஊ and leaves a stray virama, unflagged: இத்ழுறல் (202, இதழூறல்), மல்முட (205, மலமூட), மல்ருடே (210, மலரூடே).
